newsitem.title: INDIA: Germany presses India to open financial sector.
newsitem.headline: Germany presses India to open financial sector.

text.p: German Vice Chancellor Klaus Kinkel urged Indian on Friday to press ahead with economic reforms by cutting bureacratic red tape and opening its banking and insurance sectors.
"We praise the Indian government and the country for the reforms that have been carried out," Kinkel told a news conference in the Indian capital on the second day of a three-day visit.
"We would welcome it even more if liberalisation were taken one step forward. We also hope it will affect the banking and insurance sectors," he said.

Kinkel, who is accompanied by a large business delegation, said a representative of German insurance giant Allianz AG Holding had told the Indian government that his firm was interested in entering the Indian market.
"Allianz has a great interest in getting into the Indian market," said Kinkel, who is also foreign minister. "A representative asked why it has not opened up."
According to a list distributed by the German embassy, Detlev Bremkamp, a member of the board of Allianz Versicherungs AG, was in the delegation accompanying Kinkel.

Kinkel, the second highest German official after Chancellor Helmut Kohl, said he had flown to India on an Airbus Industrie jet to underscore his "enormous interest" in selling the aircraft to Air-India.

India's state-owned international carrier is considering bids to buy more than 20 aircraft valued at over $2 billion. Airbus is competing for the deal with U.S. aircraft makers Boeing Co and McDonnell Douglas Corp.

Kinkel said he was canvassing support for Airbus planes, built by a consortium of French state-owned Ste Nationale Industrielle Aerospatiale, British Aerospace Plc, Daimler-Benz Aerospace, a unit of Daimler-Benz AG, and Construcciones Aeronauticas SA of Spain.
"There is no better aircraft," Kinkel said.
Kinkel listed what he considered to be problems with the Indian economy, citing a lack of transparency, too much red tape and unspecified "customs issues".
"There is not yet free market access in the services sector," he said.
Indian Foreign Minister Inder Kumar Gujral told the same news conference that he expected bilateral economic ties to strengthen in the near future.
"In days to come, this economic relationship must be further enhanced," he said. "I am certain that in days to come this will be further strengthened.
Germany is the eight-largest foreign investor in India. Bilateral trade rose to eight billion marks in 1995 from five billion in 1991.
Kinkel said his delegation has presented a list of projects which German firms were proposing in India.

On Thursday, German executives said Siemens AG and international engineering group ABB Asea Brown Boveri AG planned to build two "showcase" steam power plants in India, taking only four years from start to finish.
